newsitem.title: GERMANY: German press calls Waigel gold grab desperate.
newsitem.headline: German press calls Waigel gold grab desperate.

text.p: German press commentators on Thursday called Finance Minister Theo Waigel's grab for Bundesbank gold a desperate move to help Bonn qualify for Europe's single currency that would not boost the economy.

"It could be that the emergency calculation makes arithmetic sense for this year, but it does not improve anything," wrote the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) daily in an editorial released ahead of publication on Friday.

Waigel said he wanted Bundesbank gold and currency reserves to be revalued from current low book prices to levels close to the normal market price, after Bonn announced a 18 billion mark ($10.6 billion) tax revenue shortfall, threatening Germany's prospects of qualifying for European monetary union (EMU).
"If there is a god of finance then he has now sent two things to the federal government: a last thunderous warning and golden manna from Frankfurt," wrote the FAZ.
Bonn's EMU bid means Waigel cannot increase new borrowing to cover the revenue shortfall without risking exceeding the three percent budget deficit to GDP Maastricht Treaty target.

Die Welt daily said Waigel was blocked from other moves because the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) would reject spending cuts to help narrow the gap and the junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) would reject higher taxes.

"All that is left is to speed up privatisation... and in addition he can hope for an economic recovery later this year, which was admittedly already expected for 1995 and then 1996," the paper wrote in its Friday editorial.

The mass circulation Bild daily said existing debts were already a burden on the country's great-grand children and said the "Waigel-wonder" in revaluing the country's gold and currency treasures could only work once.
The Neue Westfaelische Zeitung daily said Waigel had only one choice. "The only way left is to raise indirect taxes, petrol taxes and value added tax," it wrote.

Even if Bonn could turn the Bundesbank's 95 million ounces of underpriced gold into new revenue, it is not clear how it could use these funds to help meet the deficit target, but commentators said grabbing the country's gold was a surprising way to qualify for EMU.

"It shows the economic contortions that a country will manoeuvre itself into to be among the circle of nations that qualify for EMU, that what was once one of the most advanced and modern industrialised nations has to grab for the myth of a gold hoard," wrote the FAZ.

Germany has been strongly against any kind of budget fudges for EMU qualification, but record unemployment -- which Waigel said could average 4.3 million in 1997 -- means Bonn is struggling to meet the Maastricht criteria without cooking its own books.
